regions.name: Constantia
regions.summary: Constantia is the Cape's oldest fine wine address: a ward of the Cape Town district on the eastern slopes of the Constantiaberg, a short drive south of the city centre, with False Bay to the south-east and the Atlantic just over the ridge at Hout Bay. Simon van der Stel was granted the land in 1685, and by the late eighteenth century its sweet Muscat wine was poured at Europe's courts. Today the ward is cool, wet by Cape standards and best known for tense, flinty Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon. The sweet legend returned with the 1986 vintage of Klein Constantia's Vin de Constance: unfortified Muscat de Frontignan, shrivelled on the vine.

terroir.climate: Cool maritime by Cape standards, with sea on two sides. False Bay lies a few kilometres to the south-east, and the summer south-easter blows off it up the valley, cooling the afternoons and often pulling a cap of cloud over the mountain. The cold Atlantic is just over the ridge at Hout Bay. Rainfall is well above the Cape norm, most of it in winter, so mildew and rot need watching in a wet spring. The east-facing slopes lose direct sun early in the afternoon as it drops behind the Constantiaberg, which slows ripening and keeps acidity.
terroir.soils: Decomposed granite is the base: deep, well-drained loam with enough clay in the subsoil to hold winter rain into the dry months, so many blocks need little irrigation. Table Mountain sandstone caps the mountain above and has washed down over the granite on the upper slopes, leaving lighter, sandier, more acid ground. Growers credit the granite with the grip of the ward's whites and the structure of its reds.
terroir.topography: The vineyards climb the eastern and south-eastern foot slopes of the Constantiaberg, the southern arm of the Table Mountain chain, from the valley floor up towards the forest and fynbos line. The valley opens towards False Bay at Muizenberg and is closed to the west by the ridge that runs from Constantia Nek to the Constantiaberg peak. Suburban Cape Town surrounds the farms on the other sides, so the vineyard area is small and cannot grow.
terroir.water: False Bay is the ward's air conditioner: the south-easter that crosses it arrives cool and moist each summer afternoon. The cold Atlantic at Hout Bay lies just over Constantia Nek, close enough to keep nights cool. Small mountain streams feed the farm dams that supply what irrigation the ward needs.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: The ward's calling card today: flinty, green-fig, gooseberry and citrus wines with high natural acidity, often with a share of Sémillon or a little barrel work.

grapes.name: Sémillon
grapes.styles: Waxy, lemony and long-lived; bottled alone by a few farms and blended with Sauvignon Blanc into Bordeaux-style whites that age well.

grapes.name: Muscat Blanc
grapes.styles: Called Muscat de Frontignan in the Cape, the grape of Vin de Constance and Grand Constance: picked late and shrivelled on the vine for an unfortified sweet wine of apricot, orange peel and spice.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: Leads the Bordeaux-style reds on the lower granite slopes; leaner and more herbal than Stellenbosch's.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: Softens the Cabernet-led blends and makes a few varietal reds of its own.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Fine-boned, citrus-and-oatmeal wines from the cooler slopes, and base wine for Cap Classique.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: Peppery, medium-bodied Shiraz from the steep, high sites below Constantia Nek.

wines.note: The revived legend: unfortified Muscat de Frontignan, picked late after the berries shrivel on the vine, matured at length in barrel and sold in a 500 millilitre replica of the antique bottle. Apricot, candied orange peel, honey and spice on a long acid line; serve lightly chilled with foie gras, blue cheese or a fruit tart.
Groot Constantia's own revival, from red and white Muscat de Frontignan, unfortified and amber. The second answer when a guest asks for the historic wine of the valley.
Pale, flinty and taut, with gooseberry, green fig, lime and a saline finish; less tropical than Marlborough. Serve cold with oysters, crab, goat's cheese or a herb-led fish dish.
Bordeaux-style white blends, often part barrel-fermented, gaining wax, lemon curd and toast over a decade; the ward's most age-worthy dry whites. Good with richer fish, veal and cream sauces.
Cabernet Sauvignon led, with Merlot and Cabernet Franc; medium to full, more graphite and herb than flesh. Pour with lamb or beef.
Bottle-fermented sparkling wine from Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, carrying the ward's lively acidity; a fine aperitif with the oysters of the coast.

made.viticulture: Constantia's vines are trellised and mostly planted on slopes that face east or south-east, towards False Bay and away from the hot afternoon sun. The ward's rainfall and humidity make canopy management the main task: leaf removal on the morning side, open canopies for airflow and careful spraying in wet springs against downy and powdery mildew. Wind is the other constant, and the south-easter can strip leaves and break young shoots. The decomposed granite holds winter rain, so many blocks can be dry farmed. Baboons from the mountain and birds raid ripening grapes, and nets are common. Harvest runs late by Cape standards, from February for Sauvignon Blanc into March and April for Cabernet. For Vin de Constance the Muscat is left on the vine long after normal ripeness and picked in several passes as the berries shrivel and concentrate; noble rot is not the aim. The long-term hazard is the city: the vineyard area is fixed by the suburbs around it, and some historic land has been lost to housing.
made.winemaking: Sauvignon Blanc is handled reductively: cold settling, cool fermentation in stainless steel, sometimes a little skin contact or lees ageing for texture, and early bottling for the fresh style. The age-worthy whites follow Bordeaux, with partial barrel fermentation and a share of Sémillon. Vin de Constance is made from the shrivelled Muscat de Frontignan and fermented to a natural alcohol in the low teens while a great deal of the grape's sugar remains; no spirit is added. It then matures at length in barrel before bottling. The historic Constantia is generally held to have been unfortified too, which set it apart from Port, Madeira and the other sweet wines it competed with in eighteenth-century Europe. The reds follow Bordeaux too: destemmed fruit, fermentation in steel or open vats, malolactic conversion and French oak ageing. Cap Classique takes its second fermentation in the bottle in which it is sold.

law.classification: Constantia is a Wine of Origin ward, and since 2017 one of the four wards of the Cape Town district, with Durbanville, Philadelphia and Hout Bay; the district sits in the Coastal Region. A label may say Constantia only when every grape grew in the ward; Cape Town covers a blend across the four wards, and Coastal Region or Western Cape covers wider blends. Vintage and variety need 85 per cent, as everywhere in the Cape. Estate Wine and single-vineyard rules apply unchanged. Nothing in the law defines Vin de Constance or limits the grapes: the name is Klein Constantia's own, and Groot Constantia sells its sweet Muscat as Grand Constance. In the eighteenth century Constantia simply meant the wine of the estate, long before any appellation existed.
tiers: WO Coastal Region
The region above the district, used when a blend reaches beyond the Cape Town wards.
WO Cape Town
The district created in 2017 from four wards: Constantia, Durbanville, Philadelphia and Hout Bay.
WO Constantia
The ward: every grape from the Constantia valley; the name a server says.
Estate Wine
Grown, made and bottled on one registered unit; the term means the same here as across the Cape.
Single vineyard
A registered block of one variety, six hectares or less, named on the label.
labels: Klein Constantia's revived unfortified sweet Muscat de Frontignan; a wine name, not a legal category.
Groot Constantia's revived sweet Muscat, from red and white Muscat de Frontignan.
The Cape name for Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains, also called Muscadel; Muscadel is above all the fortified wine made from it elsewhere in the Cape.
The sweet wine of the Cloete era, shipped to Europe in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries.

places.name: Groot Constantia
places.note: The original farm, granted to Simon van der Stel in 1685 and divided after his death in 1712; the Cape's oldest wine-producing estate, with its Cape Dutch manor house and the Cloete cellar. Hendrik Cloete bought it in 1778 and made the sweet Constantia that reached Europe's courts; its revived sweet Muscat is Grand Constance.

places.name: Klein Constantia
places.note: The smaller portion of the original estate, higher on the slope, whose Vin de Constance revived the legend with the 1986 vintage. Its upper granite blocks also give one of the ward's reference Sauvignon Blancs.

places.name: Buitenverwachting
places.note: Afrikaans for beyond expectation, another part of van der Stel's land on the middle slopes, known for Sauvignon Blanc and a Bordeaux-style red blend.

places.name: Steenberg
places.note: At the southern end of the valley nearest False Bay, on a seventeenth-century grant: Sauvignon Blanc, Sémillon and Cap Classique are its strengths.

places.name: Constantia Nek slopes
places.note: The high, steep northern end of the valley below Constantia Nek, where Constantia Glen and Eagles' Nest farm some of the coolest, windiest sites: Bordeaux-style blends, peppery Shiraz and taut Sauvignon Blanc.

places.name: Cape Town district
places.note: The district created in 2017 to gather four wards around the city under one name: Constantia, Durbanville, Philadelphia and Hout Bay. A blend across them is labelled Cape Town.

places.name: Durbanville
places.note: The ward in the Tygerberg hills north of the city, cooled by breezes off Table Bay and the Atlantic, with much of it dry farmed. Pungent, green-edged Sauvignon Blanc is its signature, with Merlot and Pinotage beside it.

places.name: Philadelphia
places.note: The ward north of Durbanville, farther from the city and open to the Atlantic winds, with Bordeaux-style reds and Sauvignon Blanc from a small number of farms.

places.name: Hout Bay
places.note: The ward on the Atlantic side of Constantia Nek: a few small vineyards in a cool, windy bowl above the fishing harbour.

places.name: Cape Point
places.note: South of the valley around Noordhoek, the most maritime vineyards on the peninsula, open to the Atlantic; Cape Point Vineyards made the name with Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon. It is a Wine of Origin district in its own right, outside the Cape Town district, and is labelled under its own name.

producers.name: Klein Constantia
producers.why: The estate that revived Vin de Constance with the 1986 vintage, the Cape's most famous sweet wine, and a reference for Constantia Sauvignon Blanc.

producers.name: Groot Constantia
producers.why: The original estate of 1685 and the Cape's oldest wine farm, maker of Grand Constance and a full range of reds and whites.

producers.name: Buitenverwachting
producers.why: A historic Constantia farm for Sauvignon Blanc and a Cabernet-led blend.

producers.name: Steenberg
producers.why: The southern Constantia farm for Sauvignon Blanc, Sémillon and Cap Classique.

producers.name: Constantia Glen
producers.why: A high farm below Constantia Nek making Bordeaux-style red and white blends.

producers.name: Eagles' Nest
producers.why: Steep, high vineyards on the valley's northern end known for peppery Shiraz.

producers.name: Cape Point Vineyards
producers.why: The Noordhoek house whose Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon brought Cape Point onto wine lists.

producers.name: Diemersdal
producers.why: A Durbanville family farm known for Sauvignon Blanc from the cool Tygerberg hills.

exam: Vin de Constance: Klein Constantia, Muscat de Frontignan, unfortified, late-picked and shrivelled on the vine, revived with the 1986 vintage.
The history: Simon van der Stel's grant of 1685, Hendrik Cloete's sweet Constantia from 1778, Napoleon's exile on St Helena, the fall after the 1860s.
Today's dry grape: Sauvignon Blanc, cool and flinty, with Sémillon for the age-worthy blends.
The climate: False Bay's south-easter, the Atlantic over the ridge, east-facing slopes that lose the afternoon sun.
The law: a ward of the Cape Town district (2017) with Durbanville, Philadelphia and Hout Bay, in the Coastal Region.
The soils: decomposed granite, with Table Mountain sandstone capping the mountain and washed over the upper slopes.
traps: Vin de Constance is neither fortified nor botrytised: the sweetness comes from berries shrivelled on the vine.
Constantia is a ward, not a district; the district is Cape Town.
Groot Constantia is the original 1685 farm, but Klein Constantia makes Vin de Constance; Groot Constantia's sweet wine is Grand Constance.
Muscat de Frontignan is Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains, not Muscat of Alexandria, which the Cape calls Hanepoot.
Muscadel is a fortified style from the same grape; Vin de Constance is not a Muscadel.
Cape Point lies south of the valley but is a district of its own, not one of the Cape Town district's four wards.
The course note's Table Mountain sandstone is the cap over the granite, not the main vineyard soil.

cards.b: Klein Constantia's unfortified sweet wine from Muscat de Frontignan (Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains), late-picked and shrivelled on the vine, then matured in barrel. Revived with the 1986 vintage; sold in a 500 ml replica bottle.

cards.f: Historic Constantia: who made it famous
cards.b: Hendrik Cloete, who bought Groot Constantia in 1778; its sweet wine reached Europe's courts. Simon van der Stel had founded the estate in 1685, and it was divided after his death in 1712.
Powdery mildew in the mid nineteenth century, a British tariff change in the early 1860s that took away the Cape's price advantage, and from 1886 phylloxera, which ruined the vineyards.

cards.f: Constantia's place in Wine of Origin
cards.b: A ward of the Cape Town district, created in 2017, in the Coastal Region, alongside Durbanville, Philadelphia and Hout Bay.
False Bay's south-easter up the valley, the cold Atlantic just over the ridge at Hout Bay, and east-facing slopes that lose the afternoon sun behind the Constantiaberg.
Sauvignon Blanc: flinty, green fig, gooseberry, high acidity; often blended with Sémillon for age-worthy Bordeaux-style whites.

cards.f: Grand Constance: whose, and from what
cards.b: Groot Constantia's revived unfortified sweet wine from red and white Muscat de Frontignan.
Napoleon had it shipped to St Helena; Jane Austen named it in Sense and Sensibility; Dickens and Baudelaire wrote of it too.

questions.q: Which grape makes Vin de Constance?
questions.exp: Vin de Constance is made from Muscat de Frontignan, the Cape name for Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains. Muscat of Alexandria is the Cape's Hanepoot, Chenin Blanc is the national white, and Furmint is Tokaji's grape.

questions.q: In which year was Simon van der Stel granted the land at Constantia?
questions.exp: Simon van der Stel, then commander of the Cape, received the Constantia grant in 1685 and planted vines; the estate was divided after his death in 1712, giving Groot and Klein Constantia.

questions.q: How does Vin de Constance reach its sweetness?
questions.exp: The Muscat is left to shrivel on the vine and the wine is never fortified, so no spirit is added. Noble rot is not the aim, and the Cape is far too warm for ice wine.

questions.q: Which district has held the Constantia ward since 2017?
questions.exp: Wine of Origin Cape Town was created in 2017 from four wards: Constantia, Durbanville, Philadelphia and Hout Bay. Stellenbosch, Paarl and Swartland are separate districts of the Coastal Region.

questions.q: Which estate revived the sweet wine Vin de Constance with the 1986 vintage?
questions.exp: Klein Constantia, the smaller part of van der Stel's estate, revived the wine in 1986. Groot Constantia, the original farm, makes its own sweet Muscat under the name Grand Constance.

questions.q: Which white grape leads Constantia's dry wines today?
questions.exp: Cool, flinty Sauvignon Blanc is the ward's dry signature. Chenin Blanc leads the Cape as a whole, Riesling is at its best in Elgin, and Muscat of Alexandria, the Cape's Hanepoot, grows in the warm inland valleys for sweet and fortified wine.

questions.q: Which bay lies south-east of the Constantia valley and sends the summer south-easter over its vineyards?
questions.exp: False Bay lies a few kilometres to the south-east and cools the east-facing slopes each summer afternoon; the cold Atlantic at Hout Bay sits on the other side of the ridge.

questions.q: Which white grape is Sauvignon Blanc's usual partner in Constantia's age-worthy white blends?
questions.exp: Sémillon brings wax, lemon and weight to Sauvignon Blanc's acidity, the classic Bordeaux pairing, and the blends gain toast and honey over a decade. A few Constantia farms also bottle Sémillon on its own.

regions.name: Elgin
regions.summary: Elgin is the Cape's best-known cool upland district: a high basin of apple and pear orchards over the mountains from Somerset West, reached by Sir Lowry's Pass and lying a short way inland from the sea. Fruit farmers began planting vines in the 1980s, and the district now makes some of the Cape's most nervy Sauvignon Blanc, fine Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, aromatic Riesling and peppery cool-climate Syrah. Altitude, winter rain and summer cloud brought by the south-easter keep the season long and slow, so harvest comes weeks after Stellenbosch. It is a district of the Cape South Coast region, and Paul Cluver, Oak Valley, Iona and Shannon are the names to know.

terroir.climate: Cool for the Cape, and the cause is height and the sea together rather than latitude. The basin lies around 300 metres up and a short way inland from the coast, so summer days are milder than Stellenbosch's and nights are cool. The summer south-easter carries moist sea air over the mountains and often lays cloud across the valley in the afternoon, cutting sunshine hours and slowing ripening. Rainfall is high by Cape standards, falling mainly in winter, and the long, slow season brings harvest weeks after the warmer districts.
terroir.soils: Two rocks dominate. Bokkeveld shale weathers to a clay-rich, water-holding soil on the lower and middle slopes and carries much of the district's Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Sauvignon Blanc. Table Mountain sandstone forms the surrounding peaks and leaves sandier, poorer, quicker-draining soils on the higher ground. Many vineyards replaced old apple and pear blocks, on ground the orchard farmers already knew well.
terroir.topography: A high basin ringed by mountains: the range crossed by Sir Lowry's Pass to the west, the Kogelberg to the south between Elgin and the sea at Kleinmond, and further ranges to the north and east. The floor of the basin is orchard country; vineyards take the slopes around it, which face every direction. Growers choose aspect by grape: cooler south-facing blocks for Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Noir, warmer north-facing ones for Syrah and the Bordeaux varieties. Much of the valley lies within the Kogelberg Biosphere Reserve, among the fynbos of the Cape floral kingdom.
terroir.water: The Palmiet River drains the basin south to the sea near Kleinmond, and farm dams built for the orchards supply irrigation in dry spells. False Bay, beyond the western ridge, and the open ocean a short way south over the Kogelberg both lie close enough to send cool, moist air and summer cloud into the valley.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: The district's flagship white: pungent, green, citrus and flinty, with some of the Cape's highest natural acidity in the style.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Taut wines of lemon, white peach and oatmeal with fine acidity, fermented in barrel; some of the Cape's most Burgundian Chardonnay, and base wine for Cap Classique.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Red cherry, forest floor and spice, lighter and more perfumed than most Cape reds; Elgin rivals the Hemel-en-Aarde for the grape.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: Dry to off-dry wines of lime and blossom, and botrytised Noble Late Harvest; Elgin is the Cape's best-known home for true Riesling.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: Peppery, medium-bodied cool-climate Syrah, closer in feel to the northern Rhône than to the riper Shiraz of the warmer districts.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: From the warmer north-facing slopes, a few fine, fresh varietal Merlots and blends.

wines.note: Pale and tense, with lime, green pepper, passion fruit and a flinty edge; often lees-aged for texture. Serve cold with oysters, ceviche, asparagus or goat's cheese.
Barrel-fermented with restraint: lemon, white peach, hazelnut and a long, saline line. A Burgundy lover's Cape white; pour with crab, lobster, roast chicken or veal.
Light to medium-bodied, with red cherry and raspberry over earth, spice and fine tannin. Serve slightly cool with duck, salmon, mushrooms or quail.
Dry or off-dry, lime and jasmine with a firm acid spine, gaining a petrol note after a few years in bottle; good with spiced dishes, pork and Asian flavours.
Botrytised, apricot-and-marmalade sweet wine with racy acidity; serve chilled with fruit desserts, blue cheese or pâté.
Pepper, violet and black cherry with a savoury finish at moderate alcohol; for lamb, game birds or charcuterie.
High-acid Chardonnay and Pinot Noir base wines make crisp, fine bottle-fermented sparkling wine, and several houses source Elgin fruit for it.

made.viticulture: Elgin's vineyards are young by Cape standards, planted from the 1980s onward as fruit farmers looked for a second crop. Vines are trellised with vertical shoot positioning, and the orchard habits came with them: careful soil preparation, drip irrigation from farm dams in dry spells and close attention to disease. The cool, cloudy, humid summers raise the threat of downy and powdery mildew and of botrytis, so canopies are opened for airflow and sprays are timed tightly. Wind on exposed sites and the struggle to ripen late red grapes in cool years are the other hazards. Aspect decides planting: Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Noir on the cooler south-facing and higher blocks, Syrah and the Bordeaux grapes on warmer north-facing slopes. Harvest starts with sparkling base wine and Sauvignon Blanc and runs on into April for the reds, weeks behind Stellenbosch. Yields are moderate, and the best growers manage small blocks matched to soil, aspect and clone.
made.winemaking: Elgin's makers work to keep the district's natural acidity and moderate alcohol. Sauvignon Blanc is mostly fermented cool in stainless steel, often with time on the fine lees for texture, and a few are barrel-fermented or blended with Sémillon. Chardonnay is whole-bunch pressed, fermented in French oak barrels, often with native yeast, and aged on its lees with a modest share of new oak; malolactic conversion may be partial to keep its line. Pinot Noir is fermented in small open vats, some with a portion of whole bunches, punched down by hand and aged in French oak. Riesling is made in steel, dry or off-dry, and in the right autumns as Noble Late Harvest from botrytis-affected grapes. Many wineries elsewhere buy Elgin grapes and make the wine in their own cellars; the label still says Elgin when every grape grew in the district.

law.classification: Elgin is a Wine of Origin district within the Cape South Coast region, which also holds the Walker Bay, Overberg and Cape Agulhas districts among others. It is not part of the Coastal Region, despite its nearness to the sea. A stated Elgin origin must be true for every grape, wherever the wine was made; vintage and variety need 85 per cent. Estate Wine and single-vineyard rules apply as across the Cape, and the numbered Integrity and Sustainability seal on the capsule certifies origin, vintage, variety and sustainable farming. There are no grape restrictions and no site classification: the district's name rests on its climate and on the growers who matched cool grapes to it.
tiers: WO Western Cape
The geographical unit; a blend of Elgin fruit with grapes from elsewhere may fall back here.
WO Cape South Coast
The region holding Elgin, Walker Bay, Overberg, Cape Agulhas and other cool southern districts.
WO Elgin
The district: every grape grown in the Elgin basin, wherever the wine was made.
Estate Wine
Grown, made and bottled on one registered unit.
Single vineyard
One registered block of one variety, six hectares or less, named on the label.
labels: Sweet wine from botrytis-affected grapes; Elgin's Riesling is a classic source.
Bottle-fermented sparkling wine; Elgin supplies high-acid base wine for it.
The numbered Wine and Spirit Board seal certifying origin, vintage, variety and sustainable production.
On a Cape label today, true Riesling; Cape Riesling is Crouchen Blanc, a different grape.

places.name: Grabouw
places.note: The district's main town, in the middle of the basin, the hub of the apple and pear trade with its packhouses and cold stores. Most wine farms lie on the slopes within a short drive of it.

places.name: Sir Lowry's Pass
places.note: The road over the mountains from Somerset West into Elgin. The climb from the False Bay coast into the high basin explains much of the change in climate from Stellenbosch's southern farms.

places.name: Kogelberg
places.note: The mountain range between Elgin and the coast at Kleinmond, core of the Kogelberg Biosphere Reserve; its fynbos slopes close the basin to the south and the southern farms look onto it.

places.name: Houw Hoek
places.note: The pass on the eastern edge where the road leaves Elgin for Bot River, a ward of the Walker Bay district. The two are neighbours, but the district boundary between them matters on a label.

places.name: Overberg
places.note: Over the mountain: the old name for the farming country east of the Cape's first ranges, which takes in Elgin, Walker Bay and beyond. It is also a separate Wine of Origin district to the east, so a wine labelled Overberg is not an Elgin wine.

producers.name: Paul Cluver
producers.why: The family estate that pioneered wine in Elgin in the 1980s, known for Riesling, including Noble Late Harvest, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

producers.name: Oak Valley
producers.why: An old Elgin fruit farm whose Pinot Noir and Chardonnay are district references.

producers.name: Iona
producers.why: A high-lying farm known for Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir of cool precision.

producers.name: Shannon Vineyards
producers.why: Known for its Mount Bullet Merlot and Pinot Noir from the Elgin slopes.

exam: Elgin as the Cape's cool upland district: a basin around 300 metres up, near the sea, with summer cloud from the south-easter.
Apple and pear country first; vines from the 1980s, with the Paul Cluver estate the pioneer.
The grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Riesling and cool-climate Syrah.
The law: a district of the Cape South Coast region, neighbour of Walker Bay, not part of the Coastal Region.
The soils: clay-rich Bokkeveld shale on the slopes, Table Mountain sandstone higher up.
Elgin against Stellenbosch: later harvest, higher acidity, lighter wines; reached over Sir Lowry's Pass.
traps: Elgin is in the Cape South Coast region, not the Coastal Region, despite lying near the sea.
Elgin is a district in its own right, not a ward of Walker Bay; Bot River, across the Houw Hoek pass, is the Walker Bay ward.
The cooling is altitude, sea air and summer cloud, not latitude; Elgin lies barely farther south than Stellenbosch.
Cape Riesling is Crouchen Blanc; Elgin's Riesling is the true grape, which once had to be labelled Weisser or Rhine Riesling.
Many Elgin wines are made outside the district; the origin follows the grapes, not the cellar.
South Africa's Elgin shares only its name with the Speyside whisky town of Elgin in Scotland.

cards.f: Elgin: the three things that make it cool
cards.b: Altitude (a basin around 300 metres up), the nearby sea, and summer cloud carried in by the south-easter; harvest comes weeks after Stellenbosch.

cards.f: Elgin's place in Wine of Origin
cards.b: A district of the Cape South Coast region, which it shares with Walker Bay, Overberg and Cape Agulhas; not part of the Coastal Region.
Apples and pears. Fruit farmers planted vines from the 1980s; the orchards still fill the basin floor.
Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir lead; Riesling and cool-climate Syrah are rising; some Merlot on warmer slopes.
Clay-rich Bokkeveld shale on the lower and middle slopes; sandier Table Mountain sandstone on the higher ground.

cards.f: Sir Lowry's Pass: why it matters to Elgin
cards.b: It carries the road from Somerset West over the mountains into the Elgin basin. The climb explains much of the change from Stellenbosch: more height, cooler days and summer cloud.
Paul Cluver, the pioneering estate (Riesling, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir); Oak Valley; Iona; Shannon (Mount Bullet Merlot).

questions.q: Which Wine of Origin region holds the Elgin district?
questions.exp: Elgin sits in the Cape South Coast region with Walker Bay, Overberg and Cape Agulhas. The Coastal Region holds Stellenbosch and Paarl, the Breede River Valley holds Robertson, and Olifants River lies far to the north.

questions.q: Which red grape is Elgin best known for?
questions.exp: Elgin's cool, cloudy summers suit Pinot Noir, which rivals the Hemel-en-Aarde's for perfume and finesse. Pinotage and Cinsault are at their most typical in warmer districts, and late-ripening Cabernet Sauvignon struggles in Elgin's cool years.

questions.q: Which summer weather feature most sets Elgin apart from Stellenbosch?
questions.exp: The south-easter carries moist sea air over the mountains and often lays cloud across the basin, cutting sunshine and slowing ripening. Elgin's rain falls in winter, and hail and berg winds are not its mark.

questions.q: Which grape does the term Cape Riesling mean on a South African label?
questions.exp: Cape Riesling, also sold as South African or Paarl Riesling, is Crouchen Blanc, a French grape. True Riesling, once labelled Weisser or Rhine Riesling, now appears as plain Riesling, as on Elgin's labels.

questions.q: Which aromatic white grape gives Elgin's best-known Noble Late Harvest wines?
questions.exp: Elgin's cool, humid autumns favour noble rot on late-picked Riesling, and its Noble Late Harvest Riesling is among the Cape's best-known sweet wines. Elgin is the Cape's leading home for the true grape.

questions.q: Which rock weathers into the clay-rich soils of Elgin's vineyard slopes?
questions.exp: Bokkeveld shale underlies Elgin and the Hemel-en-Aarde. Malmesbury shale is the Swartland's rock, lime-rich soils mark Robertson, and the Cape has no basalt vineyards of note.

questions.q: In which decade did Elgin's fruit farmers begin planting wine grapes in earnest?
questions.exp: Fruit farmers began planting vines in the 1980s, which makes Elgin one of the younger fine wine districts of the Cape.

questions.q: In Elgin, which slope aspect gives the coolest vineyard sites?
questions.exp: South of the equator the sun tracks across the northern sky, so south-facing slopes receive the least direct sun. Elgin puts Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Noir there and Syrah on warmer north-facing blocks.

regions.name: Walker Bay / Hemel-en-Aarde
regions.summary: Walker Bay is the coastal district around Hermanus, the whale-watching town on the bay of that name south-east of Cape Town, and its heart is the Hemel-en-Aarde, the heaven-and-earth valley that climbs inland from the sea. It is the Cape's reference for Pinot Noir and Chardonnay: cool, windy and close to cold water, on clay-rich Bokkeveld shale and decomposed granite. Hamilton Russell Vineyards, founded in 1975, proved the case, and Bouchard Finlayson, Newton Johnson, Creation and Storm followed. The district holds seven wards, three of them carrying the Hemel-en-Aarde name, and sits in the Cape South Coast region.

terroir.climate: Cool maritime: the vineyards of the lower valley lie only a few kilometres from Walker Bay, and the cold sea and the strong summer south-easter keep afternoons fresh and the season long. Rain falls mostly in winter; summers are dry and windy, which limits disease but can disrupt flowering and cut yields. Moving inland and up the valley, the sea's hold weakens a little and days warm, but the wards stay among the coolest in the Cape. The wind is hazard and gift together: it keeps rot away and gives small berries with thick skins.
terroir.soils: The lower Hemel-en-Aarde Valley lies on Bokkeveld shale, weathering to a stony, clay-rich soil that holds water and gives Pinot Noir its structure and Chardonnay a firm line. Farther up the valley decomposed granite becomes more common, sandier and better drained, and growers find more perfume and a lighter frame in its wines. Table Mountain sandstone forms the ridges above. The contrast between shale and granite is the valley's own debate, argued block by block.
terroir.topography: The Hemel-en-Aarde runs inland from the coast just west of Hermanus as a narrow valley between mountain ridges, climbing from near sea level to higher ground on its upper reaches and the ridge beyond. The three Hemel-en-Aarde wards follow that climb: the Valley nearest the sea, the Upper Valley next, and the Ridge farthest inland. Bot River lies to the west, below the Houw Hoek pass that leads over to Elgin, and the Stanford wards lie to the east towards the Klein River lagoon and beyond.
terroir.water: Walker Bay, an inlet of the cold South Atlantic between Hermanus and Gansbaai, anchors the climate: its sea breeze reaches the lower valley every afternoon, and southern right whales come into it to calve in winter and spring. The Klein River lagoon east of Hermanus and the Bot River lagoon to the west are the other waters along this stretch of coast.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: The valley's red: red and dark cherry, earth, spice and a fine, firm tannin; the Cape's most Burgundian reds.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Taut, citrus and stony, barrel-fermented with restraint; the Hemel-en-Aarde's other benchmark.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: Bright, cool, flinty wines from the district's broader farms around Bot River and Stanford.

grapes.name: Pinotage
grapes.styles: Lighter, fresher, more perfumed Pinotage from cool coastal sites, with red fruit in place of smoke.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: Peppery, medium-bodied wines from the warmer Bot River farms.

grapes.name: Chenin Blanc
grapes.styles: Old vines around Bot River give rich, textured, quince-and-honey Chenin.

wines.note: Medium-bodied, with red cherry, raspberry, forest floor and spice over fine, firm tannin and bright acidity; the best age well for a decade. Serve slightly cool with duck, quail, salmon or mushroom dishes.
Citrus, white peach, hazelnut and a chalky, saline finish, fermented in French oak with restraint. Pour with lobster, crab, roast chicken or veal in cream.
Cool, flinty and citrus, with less tropical fruit than warmer Cape sites; for oysters, line fish and salads.
A lighter, more perfumed Pinotage of red fruit and gentle spice, far from the smoky, heavy style; good with grilled meats and spiced dishes.
Old-vine Chenin with quince, honey and texture from the warmer, shale-rich ward west of the valley; for pork, poultry and rich fish.
Chardonnay and Pinot Noir from the inland wards make fine, high-acid bottle-fermented sparkling wine; serve as an aperitif or with shellfish.

made.viticulture: The Hemel-en-Aarde is trellised Pinot Noir and Chardonnay country, planted fairly densely, with vertical shoot positioning and rows set to cope with the south-easter. Wind at flowering is the great hazard: it disrupts fruit set and leaves small, loose bunches, so yields are naturally low and swing sharply from vintage to vintage. The cool, dry, windy summer keeps fungal disease down, though a wet spring can bring mildew. Virus in old plant material was an early problem across the Cape, and replanting with clean vines and better Burgundian clones has lifted the valley's wines. The shale holds water, so many blocks are dry farmed or lightly irrigated. Baboons and birds take their share where the vineyards meet the fynbos. Harvest begins with sparkling base wine and runs from February into March, later on the inland wards than near the sea. Growers pick for acidity as much as sugar, and the best farms work in small blocks matched to shale or granite.
made.winemaking: The Burgundian model rules. Chardonnay is whole-bunch pressed, fermented in French oak barrels with a modest share of new wood, often with native yeast, and aged on its lees before bottling; some houses restrain malolactic conversion to keep acidity. Pinot Noir is destemmed or fermented with a portion of whole bunches in small open vats, often after a cool soak, punched down by hand and aged in French oak, again with restrained new wood. The houses prize site and bottle single-ward or single-vineyard wines, so the Valley, Upper Valley and Ridge names appear prominently on labels. Sauvignon Blanc from the wider district is fermented cool in steel, and Cap Classique follows the traditional method with its second fermentation in bottle. Hamilton Russell's discipline, bottling only Pinot Noir and Chardonnay under the estate name, set the valley's tone.

law.classification: Walker Bay is a Wine of Origin district in the Cape South Coast region. It holds seven wards: Hemel-en-Aarde Valley, Upper Hemel-en-Aarde Valley and Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge in the heaven-and-earth valley itself, with Bot River to the west, Stanford Foothills and Springfontein Rim to the east around Stanford, and the small Sunday's Glen. Hemel-en-Aarde is therefore not one appellation but the shared name of three wards; the atlas name Walker Bay / Hemel-en-Aarde joins the district to its famous valley. A ward name on the label means every grape grew in that ward; Walker Bay means the district; Cape South Coast or Western Cape covers wider blends. Vintage and variety need 85 per cent. There is no grape restriction and no ranking of sites.
tiers: WO Cape South Coast
The region above the district, shared with Elgin, Overberg and Cape Agulhas.
WO Walker Bay
The district around Hermanus; the name for a blend across its wards.
Hemel-en-Aarde Valley
The ward nearest the sea, on clay-rich shale: Hamilton Russell and Bouchard Finlayson.
Upper Hemel-en-Aarde Valley
The middle ward, farther from the sea, with more decomposed granite.
Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge
The ward farthest inland, on the high ground at the head of the valley.
Bot River, Sunday's Glen, Stanford Foothills, Springfontein Rim
The district's four other wards, outside the heaven-and-earth valley.
labels: Afrikaans for heaven and earth; the shared name of three wards, not a brand.
The district, named for the bay at Hermanus.
The region holding Walker Bay and Elgin.

places.name: Hemel-en-Aarde
places.note: The heaven-and-earth valley behind Hermanus, divided into three wards that climb inland from the sea. Together they are the Cape's answer to the question of where its Pinot Noir and Chardonnay grow best.

places.name: Hemel-en-Aarde Valley
places.note: The ward nearest the sea, a few kilometres from Hermanus, on stony, clay-rich Bokkeveld shale. Hamilton Russell Vineyards and Bouchard Finlayson are here, and it is the valley the exam means first.

places.name: Upper Hemel-en-Aarde Valley
places.note: The middle ward, farther from the sea, where decomposed granite mixes with shale; Newton Johnson is its best-known house, known for perfumed, site-specific Pinot Noir.

places.name: Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge
places.note: The ward farthest inland, on the high ground at the head of the valley, with shale and granite soils; Creation is among its houses.

places.name: Bot River
places.note: The westernmost ward, around the village of Bot River on the road to Elgin, warmer than the valley and on shale soils; old Chenin Blanc, Pinotage, Shiraz and Rhône grapes from houses such as Beaumont and Gabriëlskloof.

places.name: Stanford Foothills
places.note: Vineyards on the foothills of the Klein River mountains near the village of Stanford, east of Hermanus beyond the Klein River lagoon.

places.name: Sunday's Glen
places.note: A small ward inland of Hermanus, and one of the least seen names on a label.

places.name: Springfontein Rim
places.note: A small ward in the Stanford country south-east of Hermanus; a name to recognise on a label rather than to study.

places.name: Hermanus
places.note: The town on the bay, a fishing village turned resort, famous for southern right whales seen from its cliffs in winter and spring; the valley's wineries lie just behind it.

places.name: Cape Agulhas
places.note: The separate district to the east along the coast, around Africa's southernmost point, where the Atlantic and Indian oceans are conventionally divided. It is a neighbour of Walker Bay, not part of it.

places.name: Elim
places.note: The ward of the Cape Agulhas district near the southern tip: windswept, maritime Sauvignon Blanc, white blends and Shiraz from the southernmost vineyards in Africa.

producers.name: Hamilton Russell Vineyards
producers.why: Founded in 1975 in the Hemel-en-Aarde Valley, it proved the Cape could make serious Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, and bottles only those two under its own name.

producers.name: Bouchard Finlayson
producers.why: An early Hemel-en-Aarde Valley house founded with Burgundian partners, for Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

producers.name: Newton Johnson
producers.why: The Upper Hemel-en-Aarde Valley family house for perfumed, site-specific Pinot Noir.

producers.name: Creation
producers.why: A Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge estate known for Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

producers.name: Storm Wines
producers.why: A Pinot Noir specialist bottling a separate wine from each of the three Hemel-en-Aarde wards.

producers.name: Beaumont
producers.why: The Bot River family farm known for old-vine Chenin Blanc.

producers.name: Southern Right
producers.why: Hamilton Russell's sister label for Pinotage and Sauvignon Blanc from the district.

exam: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay: the Hemel-en-Aarde is the Cape's reference for both, with Hamilton Russell (1975) the founding name.
Hemel-en-Aarde means heaven and earth; it names three wards: Valley, Upper Valley and Ridge, in order inland from the sea.
Walker Bay is the district, in the Cape South Coast region, with seven wards including Bot River.
The climate: cool maritime, cold Walker Bay, the summer south-easter, low yields from wind at flowering.
The soils: clay-rich Bokkeveld shale in the lower valley, more decomposed granite inland.
Hermanus places it: south-east of Cape Town on the coast, famous for whales.
traps: Hemel-en-Aarde is not a brand or a single appellation; it is three wards inside the Walker Bay district.
Walker Bay is in the Cape South Coast region, not the Coastal Region.
Bot River belongs to Walker Bay, though it lies on the road to Elgin.
Elim is a ward of the separate Cape Agulhas district; its Sauvignon Blanc is not Walker Bay's.
The Hemel-en-Aarde's Pinot Noir is the Cape's most Burgundian red, but Pinotage, not Pinot Noir, is the national signature red.
Upper Hemel-en-Aarde Valley is the middle ward; the Ridge lies farthest inland.
The course line about the Atlantic at Walker Bay is right: the bay lies west of Cape Agulhas, where the two oceans are conventionally divided.

cards.f: Hemel-en-Aarde's three wards, from the sea inland
cards.b: Hemel-en-Aarde Valley nearest the sea, then Upper Hemel-en-Aarde Valley, then Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge farthest inland; all in the Walker Bay district. The name is Afrikaans for heaven and earth.
Hemel-en-Aarde Valley, Upper Hemel-en-Aarde Valley, Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge, Bot River, Sunday's Glen, Stanford Foothills, Springfontein Rim.

cards.f: Hamilton Russell Vineyards: why it matters
cards.b: Founded in 1975 in the Hemel-en-Aarde Valley; bottles only Pinot Noir and Chardonnay under its name; the house that put the valley on wine lists.
Cold Walker Bay a few kilometres away, the summer south-easter, and the climb inland onto higher ground in the upper wards.
Clay-rich Bokkeveld shale in the lower valley for structure; more decomposed granite farther inland for perfume; sandstone on the ridges above.

cards.f: Walker Bay in Wine of Origin
cards.b: A district of the Cape South Coast region, around Hermanus, with Elgin, Overberg and Cape Agulhas as neighbours.

cards.f: Wind at flowering: why it matters here
cards.b: The south-easter at flowering disrupts fruit set, so yields are low and bunches small, concentrating the Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.
A ward of the Cape Agulhas district near Africa's southern tip, east of Walker Bay; windswept Sauvignon Blanc, white blends and Shiraz.

questions.q: What does the Afrikaans name Hemel-en-Aarde mean in English?
questions.exp: Hemel is heaven and aarde is earth; the name belongs to the valley behind Hermanus and to three of Walker Bay's wards, not to any brand.

questions.q: Which two grapes made the Hemel-en-Aarde's reputation?
questions.exp: The cool maritime valley made its name with Pinot Noir and Chardonnay from 1975 onward. Chenin and Pinotage are the national grapes, Cabernet and Merlot lead Stellenbosch, and Syrah with Viognier is a Rhône pairing.

questions.q: Which Walker Bay ward sits at the inland head of the Hemel-en-Aarde valley?
questions.exp: The three Hemel-en-Aarde wards climb inland in order: the Valley nearest Hermanus, the Upper Valley in the middle and the Ridge on the high ground at the head of the valley. Bot River lies to the west, outside the valley.

questions.q: Which house, founded in 1975, first proved that the Hemel-en-Aarde could make serious Pinot Noir and Chardonnay?
questions.exp: Hamilton Russell Vineyards, in the Hemel-en-Aarde Valley ward, bottles only Pinot Noir and Chardonnay under its own name and set the Burgundian course that Bouchard Finlayson, Newton Johnson and others followed.

questions.q: Which soil gives the lower Hemel-en-Aarde Valley its stony, clay-rich character?
questions.exp: Bokkeveld shale weathers to a stony clay that holds water and gives Pinot Noir structure. Lime-rich soils mark Robertson, the Cape has no volcanic vineyards of note, and alluvial gravel lines the river valleys.

questions.q: Which Wine of Origin region contains the Walker Bay district?
questions.exp: Walker Bay shares the Cape South Coast region with Elgin, Overberg and Cape Agulhas. The Coastal Region holds Stellenbosch and Constantia, the Breede River Valley holds Robertson, and the Klein Karoo lies inland.

questions.q: Which Walker Bay ward lies farthest west, on the road towards Elgin?
questions.exp: Bot River sits beyond the Houw Hoek pass from Elgin, warmer than the Hemel-en-Aarde and known for old Chenin, Pinotage and Shiraz; it is a Walker Bay ward despite its nearness to Elgin.

questions.q: How does the strong south-easter of spring and summer most affect Hemel-en-Aarde yields?
opts: Sunburn on the bunches before harvest
questions.exp: Wind at flowering disrupts fruit set, leaving small, loose bunches and naturally low yields. Hail and spring frost are not the valley's problems, and the cool sea air limits sunburn.

regions.name: Robertson
regions.summary: Robertson is the warm inland district of the Breede River Valley, east of Cape Town beyond Worcester, where vineyards line the river between the Langeberg and the Riviersonderend mountains. It is hot and dry, irrigated from the river, and cooled by an afternoon breeze drawn up the valley from the coast. Its distinction is lime: calcareous soils, rare in the Cape, that give Robertson its name for Chardonnay and Cap Classique, from De Wetshof and Graham Beck above all. The district also grows Sauvignon Blanc, Shiraz, Colombard for brandy and everyday whites, and Red and White Muscadel, its classic fortified wine.

terroir.climate: Hot and dry by Cape standards, behind the mountains and far from the cooling Atlantic, with a small winter rainfall well short of what vines need, so irrigation is essential. Summer days are hot, but the south-easter drawn up the Breede valley from the coast brings a cooling breeze most afternoons, and nights are cooler than the daytime heat suggests, so the whites keep their acidity. Low humidity and wind keep fungal disease down, which makes the district one of the Cape's easier places to grow clean grapes.
terroir.soils: Robertson's mark is lime. Calcareous, lime-rich soils, scarce elsewhere in the Cape, lie on the slopes and terraces away from the river, often with red Karoo soil and stones; growers credit them with the freshness and fine line of the district's Chardonnay, and local lore credits them with the strong bones of the racehorses bred on the valley's stud farms. Along the Breede the soils are deep alluvial sand, loam and gravel, fertile and suited to generous crops of white grapes.
terroir.topography: A broad valley running from north-west to south-east along the Breede River, between the Langeberg mountains to the north and the Riviersonderend range to the south. Vineyards occupy the river flats, the terraces above them and the lower foot slopes, mostly at modest elevation. Side valleys run back into the mountains, the best known towards McGregor in the south, and the towns of Robertson, Ashton, Bonnievale and McGregor anchor the district.
terroir.water: The Breede River is the district's lifeline: water drawn from it and from the Brandvlei Dam upstream near Worcester runs through canals to the vineyards, and without it little would grow. The river valley also channels the cooling south-easter inland from the river's mouth on the south coast, where it meets the Indian Ocean.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: The district's signature: citrus, white peach and a fresh, chalky line from lime soils, unoaked or barrel-fermented, and the base for Cap Classique.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: Fresh, fruity wines from tropical to grassy, from the river farms and the cooler hillside sites.

grapes.name: Colombard
grapes.styles: Spelt Colombar on Cape labels: a high-acid, generous-cropping white for brandy base wine and bright everyday whites.

grapes.name: Muscat Blanc
grapes.styles: Red and white forms of Muscat de Frontignan give Muscadel, the district's classic fortified wine.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: Ripe, spicy, dark-fruited reds from the warm valley; the district's most convincing red.

grapes.name: Chenin Blanc
grapes.styles: Grown widely for everyday whites and brandy base; a few old blocks make serious dry wine.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: Ripe, soft reds from the warmer sites, often blended with Shiraz or Merlot.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Grown mainly as base wine for Cap Classique, picked early for acidity.

wines.note: From crisp and unoaked to barrel-fermented and nutty, with citrus, white peach and a fresh, chalky finish credited to the lime soils. Pour with shellfish, roast chicken or creamy pasta.

Bottle-fermented sparkling wine from Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, the district's best-known style abroad; Graham Beck's non-vintage Brut is the reference. Serve cold as an aperitif or with fried seafood.

Muscat juice fortified with grape spirit before or early in fermentation, so the wine is very sweet and grapey, with raisin, honey and orange peel. Serve lightly chilled after dinner or with nut desserts.
Ripe, spicy, dark-fruited and soft, with the warmth of the valley; good with barbecue and a South African braai.
Fresh, fruity and approachable, from tropical to grassy, an everyday glass at a fair price; for salads and grilled fish.
Bright, high-acid, lightly fruity white, often off-dry; also the base wine for much South African brandy.

made.viticulture: Robertson's vineyards are irrigated by necessity, and the canals from the Breede and the Brandvlei Dam shape where and what is planted: generous-cropping whites on the fertile river flats, and lower-yielding Chardonnay, Shiraz and Sauvignon Blanc on the lime-rich slopes and terraces, where growers can ration water. Vines are trellised, often in wide rows for machines on the flats, and bush vines survive in a few old blocks of Chenin Blanc and Muscadel. The hot, dry climate means little fungal disease, so the district suits organic and low-spray farming better than the wet coastal wards. The hazards are heat, sunburn on exposed bunches and water supply in drought years, when allocations from the dam are cut. Harvest is early by Cape standards, starting in January for sparkling base wine and Sauvignon Blanc and running through February and March. Picking at night or at dawn keeps the fruit cool for the whites. The district is one of the Cape's larger producers by volume, with cooperative cellars alongside family estates.
made.winemaking: Chardonnay is the cellar's centre: unoaked versions fermented cool in steel for freshness, and premium versions whole-bunch pressed and fermented in French oak with lees stirring and a measured share of new wood. Cap Classique follows the traditional method: base wines of Chardonnay and Pinot Noir picked early for acidity, a second fermentation in the bottle and extended time on the lees before disgorging; the leading houses keep reserve wines and release vintage and prestige cuvées. Muscadel is made by adding grape spirit to the sweet juice before or early in fermentation, keeping almost all the sugar, and it may rest in old casks for years. Colombard and Chenin Blanc grown for brandy are made into a light, acidic base wine for distilling. The reds are fermented in steel or open tanks and aged in French and American oak.

law.classification: Robertson is a Wine of Origin district within the Breede River Valley region, which also holds the Worcester and Breedekloof districts upstream. Its wards include McGregor, Bonnievale, Klaasvoogds, Eilandia, Le Chasseur, Agterkliphoogte, Boesmansrivier, Hoopsrivier and Vinkrivier, each a named locality of shared soil and climate, though most wines simply say Robertson. A district or ward origin must be true for every grape; vintage and variety need 85 per cent. Muscadel is the Cape's name for fortified wine from Muscat de Frontignan, and Cap Classique requires a second fermentation in the bottle. The marketing name Robertson Wine Valley, the valley of wine and roses, is a trade slogan and not an origin.
tiers: WO Western Cape
The geographical unit, for blends beyond the valley.
WO Breede River Valley
The region: the Robertson, Worcester and Breedekloof districts along the river.
WO Robertson
The district: every grape grown within it; the name on most labels.
Wards
McGregor, Bonnievale, Klaasvoogds, Eilandia, Le Chasseur and others: local names inside the district, used on single-site wines.
Estate Wine
Grown, made and bottled on one registered unit.
labels: Fortified sweet wine from red or white Muscat de Frontignan; Robertson and the Klein Karoo are its homes.
The district's trade name and slogan, not an origin.

places.name: Robertson town
places.note: The district's centre on the Breede, a farming town with cellars and estates on its edges; De Wetshof's lime-rich Chardonnay slopes and Graham Beck's Cap Classique cellar both lie in the surrounding valley.

places.name: Bonnievale
places.note: A ward and town downstream to the south-east, among the river's bends; known for Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc, with Weltevrede among its family estates.

places.name: McGregor
places.note: A ward in a side valley south of Robertson towards the Riviersonderend mountains, quieter and a little cooler, with Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc and Shiraz.

places.name: Klaasvoogds
places.note: A ward on the Langeberg side of the valley between Robertson and Ashton, with hillside sites on stony, lime-touched ground.

places.name: Ashton
places.note: The town east of Robertson at the foot of the Langeberg, home to cooperative cellars and the gateway to the pass that leads to Montagu.

places.name: Worcester and Breedekloof
places.note: The upstream districts of the same region: Worcester, a large volume producer and the Cape's brandy centre, and Breedekloof, wetter and known for Chenin Blanc. They share the Breede and the Breede River Valley label with Robertson.

places.name: Klein Karoo
places.note: The separate region farther east and inland beyond the Langeberg, where Calitzdorp makes the Cape's best-known port-style wines and Muscadel is also at home; it is not part of Robertson.

producers.name: Graham Beck
producers.why: The Robertson Cap Classique specialist whose non-vintage Brut was poured at Nelson Mandela's inauguration in 1994.

producers.name: De Wetshof
producers.why: A family Chardonnay specialist on the lime soils, among the Cape's pioneers of the grape.

producers.name: Springfield Estate
producers.why: A family farm on stony river soils known for Sauvignon Blanc and a wild-yeast Chardonnay.

producers.name: Bon Courage
producers.why: A family estate for Cap Classique, Muscadel and Chardonnay.

producers.name: Weltevrede
producers.why: A Bonnievale family estate devoted to Chardonnay from its different soils.

producers.name: Rietvallei
producers.why: A family estate known for Red Muscadel from very old vines.

producers.name: Van Loveren
producers.why: A large family wine business with a broad range from the valley, a common name by the glass.

exam: Robertson's lime-rich soils, rare in the Cape, and its name for Chardonnay.
Cap Classique: Graham Beck as the reference house, its Brut poured at the 1994 inauguration.
The climate: hot and dry, irrigated from the Breede River, cooled by the afternoon south-easter up the valley.
The law: a district of the Breede River Valley region, with Worcester and Breedekloof upstream.
Muscadel: fortified Muscat de Frontignan, red and white, a Robertson speciality.
Robertson against Stellenbosch: inland, warmer, irrigated, white and sparkling first.
traps: Robertson is in the Breede River Valley region, not the Coastal Region and not the Cape South Coast.
Lime here means calcareous soil, not citrus; the course note's lime soils are limestone-rich ground.
Muscadel is fortified; Constantia's Vin de Constance, from the same grape, is not.
Robertson is warm, yet it is a white and sparkling district first: lime soils and the afternoon breeze explain it.
Colombard appears on Cape labels as Colombar.
Most Robertson wines say only Robertson; the ward names a server meets most often are Bonnievale, McGregor and Klaasvoogds.

cards.b: Lime-rich soils rare in the Cape; Chardonnay and Cap Classique; a hot, dry, irrigated valley cooled by the afternoon south-easter.
A district of the Breede River Valley region, with Worcester and Breedekloof upstream; wards include McGregor, Bonnievale, Klaasvoogds and Eilandia.

cards.f: Graham Beck: why a sommelier knows it
cards.b: Robertson's Cap Classique reference house; its non-vintage Brut was poured at Nelson Mandela's inauguration in 1994.
The Cape's fortified sweet wine from red or white Muscat de Frontignan, with grape spirit added before or early in fermentation; a Robertson and Klein Karoo speciality.
The Breede River and the Brandvlei Dam upstream near Worcester, by canal; rainfall is far too low for dry farming.

cards.f: The mountains on each side of Robertson
cards.b: The Langeberg to the north, the Riviersonderend range to the south; the Breede runs between them.
De Wetshof, the lime-soil pioneer; Graham Beck for Cap Classique; Springfield and Weltevrede for still wines.

questions.q: Which soil type sets Robertson apart from most Cape districts?
questions.exp: Robertson's lime-rich calcareous soils are scarce elsewhere in the Cape and underpin its Chardonnay. Decomposed granite marks much of Stellenbosch, Malmesbury shale the Swartland, and Table Mountain sandstone the high mountain slopes.

questions.q: Which river runs through the Robertson district and supplies its irrigation?
questions.exp: Canals from the Breede and the Brandvlei Dam upstream water the valley; the river also channels the cooling south-easter inland from the south coast.

questions.q: Which Wine of Origin region holds the Robertson district?
questions.exp: Robertson shares the Breede River Valley region with Worcester and Breedekloof. The Coastal Region holds Stellenbosch, the Cape South Coast holds Elgin and Walker Bay, and the Klein Karoo is a separate region farther east.

questions.q: Which grape is Robertson's signature on its lime-rich slopes?
questions.exp: Chardonnay, still and as Cap Classique base, is the district's calling card. Pinotage is Stellenbosch's crossing, Chenin is grown everywhere, and Cabernet leads the coastal districts.

questions.q: Which Robertson house's non-vintage Brut was poured at Nelson Mandela's 1994 inauguration?
questions.exp: Graham Beck is Robertson's Cap Classique reference, making bottle-fermented sparkling wine from Chardonnay and Pinot Noir grown on the valley's lime-rich soils.

questions.q: How is Robertson's Muscadel made?
opts: Grape spirit added to the must
questions.exp: Grape spirit added to the sweet must stops or prevents fermentation, so the Muscat's sugar stays and the wine is very sweet. Straw drying is the passito method, botrytis makes Noble Late Harvest, and bottle fermentation makes Cap Classique.

questions.q: Which term do South African labels use for the bottle-fermented sparkling wine that is Robertson's best-known style abroad?
questions.exp: Cap Classique, also written Méthode Cap Classique, is the Cape's term for traditional-method sparkling wine, with its second fermentation in the bottle; Chardonnay and Pinot Noir from Robertson's lime soils make some of the best.

questions.q: Which wind cools Robertson's vineyards on summer afternoons?
opts: The berg wind from the interior
The Atlantic breeze off the west coast
questions.exp: The south-easter is drawn up the Breede valley from the south coast and tempers the afternoon heat. Berg winds bring heat, the north-wester brings winter rain, and the Atlantic breeze cools the west-coast districts, far beyond Robertson's mountains.
